After seeing my folding bike, a friend of mine decided he wanted a folder of his own, but couldn't afford one at the time. So he saved up and recently bought himself a brand new Dahon. He let me try it out, and when I was riding it, I noticed a squeaking noise. Because the bike was new, we felt 99% sure it wasn't any of the hinges or bearings. Being the foolish amateur bike mechanic that I am, I suggested that we try and diagnose the problem ourselves, and he agreed.

The first thing we did was grease the saddle rails and the post, since that's a common culprit and one of the easiest fixes. No change. Then we took the handlebar clamp apart and greased that. Nothing. Then we greased the bit of stem that adjusts up or down. Still no change. We both noted that the squeaking was plastic sounding, so we took off the plastic fenders that come on the bike. Still no change. Then we noticed that it was only happening while pedaling, so we swapped out the cheap plastic folding pedals that come with the bike for a set of equally cheap plastic non-folding pedals I had saved from another bike. Still no change. We were starting to get frustrated, but that's when we finally found the problem.

On the seat post clamp, there's this skinny little brass colored curved rectangular washer that sits between the quick release lever and the clamp itself. It's much smaller than the fat concave washers you'll often see on a quick release. We unscrewed the quick release bolt and greased both sides of that little washer. It completely removed all the annoying squeaking noises. My guess is that they were supposed to add grease to that part when the bike was assembled and whoever was responsible just forgot. It's amazing how that tiny sliver of metal was causing such loud and annoying creaking noises.

Figuring out creaks and squeaks on a bike can be a time consuming and occasionally expensive process of elimination. Hopefully some of this post will save somebody a little frustration. If you take something away, it's that sometimes the solution is as simple as adding a little grease to the right part(s).
